USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture — keep the $250B of Section 301 tariffs already in force and the scheduled January 1 escalation to 25% on List 3 as leverage, but do not push toward the further $267B (List 4) that would cover virtually all remaining Chinese imports. Signal openness to serious talks conditioned on China making structural concessions on technology transfer and market access, without offering new commitments ourselves ahead of the midterms. Avoid both maximal escalation and any premature rollback.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate, not existential: the American economy is in strong shape at the decision date — industrial production rising to 104.1 (Sep), consumer sentiment at a robust 100.1, the broad dollar up ~5.5% over the window, and the Fed funds rate at 1.95% in a tightening cycle (country_health) — so the dispute is not yet dragging domestic GDP. But it is not an unalloyed opportunity either: China's Sept 24 retaliation ($60B, 5–10%) pushed duties onto 85%+ of US exports, deliberately targeting politically pivotal farm states (soybeans/pork in Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri), and the administration has had to float a $12B farm-aid package, which signals real domestic/political cost heading into the Nov midterms (web_search: columbiadailyherald 2018-09-18; usatoday 2018-09-18). The balance of motivation for escalation is thinning: the US already covers ~half of Chinese imports, an additional $267B List 4 would raise consumer prices broadly right before the midterms, and the scheduled Jan 1 bump from 10% to 25% already preserves leverage without further action. Given the US economy holds the stronger hand while China's is slowing (Lexology/NYT 2018-09-17), the disciplined move is to hold pressure and talk — escalation beyond what is already banked risks supply-chain and consumer-price shock and market/ally friction disproportionate to any added leverage at this juncture.
key_factors: US macro strength at decision date (IP 104.1, sentiment 100.1, dollar +5.5%, fed funds 1.95%) argues threat is contained
~$250B of Section 301 tariffs in force; List 3 at 10% (Sept 24) scheduled to rise to 25% Jan 1, 2019 — leverage already banked
China retaliated Sept 24 with $60B duties covering 85%+ of US exports, targeting soybeans/pork in swing farm states
Midterm political exposure: $12B farm-aid package signals material political cost in the rural base
Further escalation to $267B (List 4) would cover all remaining Chinese imports and broaden consumer-price and market risk
Negotiations (Liu He visit) derailed by the $200B action; both sides continue 'fight and talk' posture

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the retaliatory line already in place but do not escalate further; keep the door open to a new round of talks (Liu He/Wang Shouwen delegation) aimed at forestalling the Jan 1, 2019 jump of the $200B List 3 tariff from 10% to 25%. Escalating further would hand Washington the pretext for phase three ($267B, covering nearly all Chinese exports), while full concession would surrender leverage with no guarantee of relief. The right posture is firm, reciprocal, but engagement-oriented.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high and rising: as of Sept 24 the US has Section 301 tariffs live on ~$250B of Chinese imports (~half of China's annual exports to the US), with the $200B tranche scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% on Jan 1 (timeline entries 2018-09-17/18/24; USTR Sept 18 finalization) and a threatened phase-three $267B that would cover essentially all of China's ~$506B in exports (NYT 9/17; Politico 9/18). China has retaliated tit-for-tat ($34B, $16B, then 5-10% on $60B on Sept 24), but it is running low on US import value (~$130B) to counter, and analysts flag that the trade war hits China's more export-dependent economy harder than the US (CNBC 9/19; CNN 9/18). The RMB has already fallen ~8-9% since April, and Beijing has publicly ruled out currency devaluation as a weapon, capping one key offset (Sun Zhigang/Li Keqiang comments, CNN Money 9/19/20). The yuan depreciation, US dollar strength, and rising US 10-yr/2-yr yields (DGS10 to ~3.06-3.10%, DGS2 to ~2.83% by late Sept) bracket a tightening external environment. This is squarely a +0.5-high or worse situation on the CHN scale — major export exposure and firm-level/tech targeting (recall ZTE denial order, 4/16) — so +0.6 reflects the live escalation and the pending 25% step-up. On action, further escalation is not in China's interest: it would trigger phase three and hurt the multinationals and FDI China depends on, and China cannot match dollar-for-dollar. Yet with Beijing's stated line that 'the only correct way to solve the dispute is through talk and consultation on the basis of equity' (Geng Shuang, Politico/FT 9/18) and its review of the Liu He trip, engaging in talks without new concessions is the disciplined stance — hence action_score near zero-positive and action_level = negotiate.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese exports now covered by US Section 301 tariffs, with the $200B tranche set to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019
Threatened phase-three $267B would cover essentially all ~$506B of China's US exports
China's retaliation capacity is limited (~$130B of US imports to target) and it has ruled out currency devaluation
RMB already down ~8-9% since April amid dollar strength and higher US yields
Tech/firm-level targeting precedent (ZTE denial order) adds strategic threat
Beijing keeps open the talks path (Liu He delegation review) as its preferred de-escalation channel
